title: Choose the visual world for riah.dev
question: The roll assigned the Operations Wall. Keep it, take an alternate, or re-roll.

options.label: The Operations Wall
options.thesis: The site is RIAH's operations wall: each service is a live screen showing the system it keeps running.
materials: deep slate wall that owns whole regions
bright framed display panels with title bars
status lights: green OK, amber failover
options.viewport: Slate wall. Left: huge headline saying what RIAH does in plain words, one blue action. Right: six live panels (uplinks, firewall, servers, SMS, payments, DHIS2) with ticking illustrative data.
options.risk: Can read as a software dashboard product if copy is vague; demo numbers must be labelled illustrative.

raised.raise: Total palette commitment: slate owns whole bands of the page, panels snap to whole grid units.
Every panel wears a title bar naming the service and its status, so no block is ever unlabelled.
Delivery runs as fixed stations (audit, design, test, deploy, support) with a marker showing where a project is.

options.label: The Transit Map
options.thesis: Each service is a coloured line; each sector is a route you can follow across the city of RIAH's work.
options.viewport: A big full-width map: pick 'health programme' or 'bank' and its route lights up through the services it uses.
options.risk: Familiar trope, and the closest to the diagram you found confusing.

options.label: The Control Desk
options.thesis: Services as physical keys on a control surface; one orange key is the consultation.
options.viewport: A keyboard-like grid of service keys; pressing one shows its detail on a small amber screen.
options.case: Very scannable grid, but reads as a gadget brand more than an infrastructure firm.
options.risk: Ministries and NGOs may not see themselves in a hardware toy.

options.label: Azulejo Station Hall
options.thesis: Services as cobalt-painted tile panels in sequence.
options.case: Not the audience's world; adds no clarity.
options.kept: Total palette commitment and whole-unit grid.

options.label: One-bit Desktop
options.thesis: Services as windows on a dithered desktop.
options.case: Retro novelty undermines trust for enterprise buyers.

options.label: Darkroom Safelight Bay
options.thesis: Work emerging station by station under amber light.
options.case: No link to networks or payments.
options.kept: Fixed stations with progress markers for the delivery process.

options.label: Japanese High-Density Web
options.thesis: Every service packed into a ruled module mosaic.
options.case: Density makes it harder for non-engineers, the opposite of your feedback.
options.kept: Every module carries its own header tab.

options.label: Pickling Brine Calendar
options.thesis: Services as jars maturing on a shelf.
options.case: Unrelated to the audience and the offer.
options.kept: Each item banded with its state and time.

canonCard.label: The category standard
canonCard.thesis: A classic corporate IT-services site, executed well.
canonCard.viewport: Large photo of infrastructure with headline over it, two buttons, then a grid of service cards.
canonCard.risk: Looks like every other IT firm; needs real photos you don't have yet.
